newsitem.title: GERMANY: German/Swiss link in Deutsche Telekom rival.
newsitem.headline: German/Swiss link in Deutsche Telekom rival.

text.p: Swiss Telecom PTT and two regional German utilities on Tuesday outlined plans for a cross-border venture that would create Germany's first regional phone company and a new local rival for Deutsche Telekom AG.

While the venture is small compared with the mega-deals of the world's global telecoms operators, it highlights the importance of regional economic ties in the development of Europe's new telecommunications landscape after market deregulation in 1998, analysts said.

The new company, Communications Network Services (CNS), will offer communications services to businesses and later residential customers in southwestern Baden-Wuerttemberg state, which shares borders with Switzerland and France.
Swiss Telecom, a monopoly at home, will hold 50 percent of CNS and a holding company owned by utilities Energie-Versorgung Schwaben AG (EVS) and Badenwerk AG will hold the rest.

The CNS partners plan to invest 300 million marks ($185 million) over the next five years and predicted that the company would break even by 2002 to become the second most important operator in the state.
Company officials, at a news conference to outline the deal, joked how ambitions to merge regional economic interests of the Swiss and their German neighbours existed for centuries.
"Napoleon wanted to merge Baden and Switzerland," said EVS board member Ernst Hagemeyer. "What politicians couldn't do we will accomplish in the area of telecommunications."

While their ambitions are on a smaller scale, CNS believes there is a business niche for local operators to provide communications for German and Swiss enterprises that carry out some 20 billion marks in regional trade each year.

The region hosts some of Germany's most important mid-sized engineering companies and industry titans like Daimler-Benz AG, Robert Bosch GmbH, Porsche AG as well as major universities and research facilities.
"Traditionally the German-Swiss border region is one of the most developed and dynamic economic regions in Germany," said Felix Rosenberg, general director of state-owned Swiss Telecom.

For Swiss Telecom, which itself will be transformed into a joint stock company when Switzerland opens its telecoms market, the venture is part of a strategy to extend its home market by forming partnerships with operators in neighbouring regions.
"Our goal is to expand into flourishing economic areas. France is interesting as is the Lombardy region in Italy. We will be doing something there," said Rosenberg.

Swiss Telecom is a 25 percent shareholder in the Unisource NV alliance with telecoms companies from Spain, Sweden and the Netherlands and Unisource is a partner of AT&T Corp in Germany with Mannesmann, a main Telekom rival.

Although a regional phone company at first seems like a communications island surrounded by looming continents, its strength is that it has far-reaching local networks and ties to local customers that newcomers will need years to duplicate, analysts said.
Combined with the international reach through Unisource, CNS could become a powerful player on its home turf.
Michael Gassner, head of Badenwerk's telecoms activities, said competitors such as Mannesmann or energy group Veba AG were far too optimistic about entering local markets.

"In some data services markets we expect to be able to get up to 20 percent market share," he said. "We believe that in addition to us there is only room for one more competitor to Deutsche Telekom in Baden-Wuerttemberg."
Separately, Colt Telecom said it planned to build a 100 million mark fibre optic network to provide corporate phone services in Munich.
The unit of Britain's Colt Telecom Group Plc has already built a telecom network in Frankfurt and expects to build similar fibre optic systems in Hamburg and Berlin this year.
-- William Boston, Stuttgart newsroom, 49 711 6197355 ($1=1.6223 Mark)
